plan.title: Whole-blood case/control cohort: sample subgroup discovery
plan.analytical_narrative: The 120 whole-blood samples (60 case, 60 control; single Salmon-derived gene-count batch) are examined for structure beyond the labeled case/control split. Track 1 runs the standard sample-structure QC (blind VST, PCA on the top 500 variable genes, sample-distance heatmap) that the knowledge base requires before any count-data analysis, and filters low-count genes with edgeR's filterByExpr. Track 2 answers the central question with unsupervised consensus clustering (ConsensusClusterPlus) on the top 2000 most variable variance-stabilized genes, testing k=2..6 and selecting k from the consensus CDF delta-area and the proportion of ambiguous clustering (PAC), per the grounded procedure for sample subgroup discovery. Because a data-driven cluster is only a hypothesis until checked against confounders, the same track cross-tabulates any discovered clusters against the known case/control label, library size, and (if present) other processing variables, and separately runs MCP-counter immune/stromal composition scores so that a 'subgroup' driven purely by blood cell composition can be told apart from one that is not. A supervised cross-validated classifier (penalized logistic regression, nested CV) is NOT run, because the research question is descriptive discovery of latent structure, not prediction of the known case/control label — adding a classifier would be unasked scope. All numeric assumptions (gene counts, sample counts, resampling parameters) are grounded in the actual 12000x121 count matrix and 60/60 design. The final report states the discovered number of clusters, their stability (item consensus, cluster consensus, PAC), and whether any cluster aligns with case/control status, library size, or immune composition — with the explicit caution that consensus clustering finds apparent structure even in unstructured data, so any cluster is reported as a hypothesis pending independent replication, not a validated subtype.

flags.message: A quantifier name alone does not establish that the length correction occurred. If the counts come from Salmon, kallisto, or RSEM as a gene-level table, with no per-sample quantification files and no average transcript length table, the import state is not established. Ask for the per-sample quantification files, quant.sf, abundance.h5, or genes.results, or for the average transcript length table per gene and sample. If neither arrives, fit the count model on the counts as delivered, with no length offset, and state in the plan and in the report that the length offset is lost and that a change in isoform use can show as differential expression. Do not run tximport on a gene table, because tximport imports transcript estimates, and do not invent a length input.

If each group holds 50 or more samples, use limma-voom with a fixed-effects linear model for the differential expression test. In a population cohort the sample-to-sample variation does not obey the negative binomial model, and DESeq2 and edgeR then report many false positives, even on permuted labels. The linear model on the log counts with precision weights keeps the false discovery rate closer to the nominal level than the count models, but it also exceeds it on some data. The paper recommends the Wilcoxon rank-sum test at a large sample size. State this caution in the report, and give the Wilcoxon test or a permutation check as the control.

If fewer than about 50 genes pass the significance threshold, do not run an over-representation test on that list. A hypergeometric test of a short list finds no category, and a change of the threshold changes the list and the result. Run the ranked method on the full list of tested genes instead, because it finds a set of genes with a small but coordinated change that no single gene shows. State the size of the significant list in the report.
